slides.title: What is a proposition?
slides.kicker: Statements math can judge true or false
bullets: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both and never neither.
Book's Statement 1: if two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
Only statements that can be judged true or false count, so a question or a request is not a proposition.
slides.note: True ya false — proposition ke beech koi middle ground nahi!

slides.title: Meet the converse
slides.kicker: Swap the if part and the then part
bullets: The converse of 'if X then Y' is 'if Y then X' — the two parts simply trade places.
Book's Statement 2: if two angles of a triangle are equal, the opposite sides have equal lengths — the converse.
'If X then Y' can also be written as 'X implies Y', and the book uses both formulations interchangeably.

left.title: Proposition
items: Two equal sides, so opposite angles equal

right.title: Converse
items: Two equal angles, so opposite sides equal

slides.note: Converse banane ka funda: X aur Y ki jagah swap karo!

slides.title: True, but converse?
slides.kicker: A true proposition does not guarantee its converse
bullets: The chapter's big question: if a proposition is true, is its converse always true?
Book's Example 1: 'if it rains, then the road is wet' is true, but the converse 'if the road is wet, then it has rained' may not be.
The road may be wet because a tanker spilled water on it — so the converse fails in that situation.

left.title: Proposition P: true
items: If it rains, then the road is wet

right.title: Converse Q: not always
items: If the road is wet, then it has rained
A tanker could have spilled the water

slides.note: Road geeli hai, par barish zaroori nahi — tanker bhi gira sakta hai!

slides.title: Counterexamples rule
slides.kicker: One example can fell a whole claim
bullets: A counterexample is a situation that illustrates why a given proposition is not necessarily true — it contradicts the stated proposition.
Finding a suitable counterexample is an important ingredient of mathematics: it shows a proposition is false in a short and convincing way.
Book's Example 2: every multiple of 6 is a multiple of 3, yet 3 itself is a multiple of 3 that is not a multiple of 6.

items: Claim: every multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6
Try 3: a multiple of 3, but not of 6

slides.note: Ek counterexample = poora claim out!

slides.title: Fermat meets Euler
slides.kicker: A famous claim felled by one number
bullets: Fermat claimed that all numbers of the form 2^(2^n)+1 are prime, for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on.
For example, 257 is a number of this form, and it is prime.
Euler disproved the claim by showing that another number of this form is composite — one counterexample was enough.
slides.note: Bade mathematician bhi galat ho sakte hain — proof hi boss hai!

slides.title: Factor-partner pairs
slides.kicker: Every factor carries a partner along
bullets: Each factor has a partner factor: 5 is a factor of 35, and 5 × 7 = 35, so 7 is the partner of 5.
For the number 12, the factor-partner pairs are (1, 12), (2, 6) and (3, 4).
Pairing factors like this will unlock a lovely secret about squares and factor counts.
slides.note: Har factor ka ek partner — jodi banate chalo!

slides.title: Odd factors mean square
slides.kicker: The chain that proves the converse claim
bullets: The book's chain: n has an odd number of factors, so some factor-partner pair repeats as (f, f), so n = f × f is a square.
Like the partner of 5 in 25: the pair (5, 5) repeats, and 25 = 5 × 5.
If no pair repeats, every factor has a distinct partner, so the number of factors is even.
slides.note: Odd ginti? Koi factor khud ka hi partner ban gaya!

slides.title: Squares have odd factors
slides.kicker: Only one self-pairing partner is possible
bullets: For the other direction, start at the end of the chain: n = f × f clearly gives the repeating pair (f, f).
But a repeating pair does not by itself force an odd count: two repeating pairs (f, f) and (g, g) would give an even number of factors.
A number cannot have more than one factor pair with repeating factors, so a square number necessarily has an odd number of factors.

items: n is a square: n = f × f
A second repeating pair is impossible
So the factor count is odd

slides.note: Do self-partner jodiyan? Sirf ek hi mumkin!

slides.title: A two-way street
slides.kicker: Perfect square and odd factors imply each other
bullets: In Example 3, 'n is a perfect square' and 'n has an odd number of factors' imply each other.
So here both the proposition P and its converse Q are true — a genuinely two-way implication.
The chapter's lesson: a proposition can be true without its converse, or both can be true together.

left.title: P true, Q false
items: If it rains, the road is wet
Wet road means it rained? No

right.title: P and Q both true
items: Perfect square, so odd number of factors
Odd number of factors, so perfect square

slides.note: Kabhi ek tarafda, kabhi dono tarafda — dono possible!

slides.title: Same area, congruent?
slides.kicker: Book's Example 4 tests both directions
bullets: Proposition P: if two triangles have the same area, then they are congruent.
Converse Q: if two triangles are congruent, then they have the same area.
Congruent triangles always share one area, but two triangles can share an area yet have different side lengths — test P with such a pair.
slides.note: Area barabar, par shape alag ho sakti hai!

slides.title: Baudhāyana–Pythagoras
slides.kicker: The right-triangle statement in if-then form
bullets: Let a, b, c be the sidelengths of a triangle: if the triangle is right-angled, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
This is the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, written as a proposition of the form if X then Y.
Here X is 'the triangle is right-angled' and Y is 'a^2 + b^2 = c^2'.
slides.note: Right angle ho toh sides ka hisaab pakka!

slides.title: Writing the converse
slides.kicker: Keep the first sentence, flip the second
bullets: To write the converse, keep the first sentence of the theorem as it is and make the necessary change in the second.
Converse: let a, b, c be the sidelengths of a triangle; if a^2 + b^2 = c^2, then the triangle is right-angled.
The natural question now: is this converse true?
slides.note: Pehla sentence waisa hi, doosra ulta — converse ready!

slides.title: Converse proved true
slides.kicker: SSS congruence seals the argument
bullets: Take triangle ABC with sidelengths a, b, c and a^2 + b^2 = c^2; picture a right-angled triangle XYZ with legs a and b.
By the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem applied to XYZ, the hypotenuse satisfies XY^2 = a^2 + b^2 = c^2, so XY = c.
All three sides match, so ABC and XYZ are congruent by the SSS criterion — ABC had to be a right triangle after all.

items: Right triangle XYZ with legs a, b

slides.note: SSS ne kaam kar dikhaya — converse bhi sach!

slides.title: When means if
slides.kicker: Same meaning in a new dress
bullets: 'If X then Y' is not the only wording; 'Y when X' conveys the same meaning.
'A number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square' says the same thing as the if-then version from Example 3.
So while reading propositions, watch for when and other sentence structures that hide an if-then.

left.title: If-then form
items: If a number is a perfect square, then it has an odd number of factors

right.title: When form
items: A number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square

slides.note: When dikhe toh if-then samjho!

slides.title: A proposition at the incentre
slides.kicker: Bisectors meet, then a neat if-then claim
bullets: Given any triangle ABC, bisect the angles at B and C; the bisectors meet at the incentre I of the triangle.
Now extend the bisectors beyond I till they meet the opposite sides at E and F.
The book's proposition: if AB = AC, then IE = IF.

items: If AB = AC then IE = IF

slides.note: Incentre = angle bisectors ka adda!

slides.title: Equations think if-then
slides.kicker: The move you use every single time
bullets: Proposition: if x = y, then a + x = a + y, where x, y and a are any three numbers.
This proposition and its converse are routinely used while solving equations.
Adding the same number to both sides keeps an equation balanced — that is the if-then logic at work.
slides.note: Equation solve karte waqt if-then hi chal raha hota hai!

slides.title: Prime generators fail
slides.kicker: No neat expression makes only primes
bullets: There are no known 'neat' expressions that generate only primes.
The exercise lists claims to test: all numbers of the form 4n^2 + 1, or n^2 + n + 11, or 4^n + 3 are prime.
Also on trial: if n is prime then 2^n - 1 is prime, and if n is even then 2^n + 1 is prime.
slides.note: Formula dekh ke prime mat maano — test karo!

slides.title: Felling the prime claims
slides.kicker: Two worked counterexamples from the exercise
bullets: Claim: n^2 + n + 11 is always prime. At n = 10 it gives 100 + 10 + 11 = 121 = 11 × 11, which is composite.
Claim: if n is prime then 2^n - 1 is prime. At n = 11 it gives 2047 = 23 × 89, which is composite.
In each case a single value of n contradicts the claim, so the claim is false.
slides.note: n = 10 aur n = 11 — chhote numbers, bade claims gaye!

slides.title: The divisibility converse trap
slides.kicker: A converse trap hiding in divisibility
bullets: True proposition: if a number is divisible by 8, then it is divisible by both 2 and 4.
Justify it: n = 8 × k = 2 × (4k) and also n = 4 × (2k), so divisibility by 2 and by 4 both follow.
The converse fails: 12 is divisible by 2 and by 4 but not by 8, so checking 2 and 4 is not enough for 8.

right.title: Divisible by 2 and 4
items: 12 = 2 × 6 = 4 × 3, yet 12 is not a multiple of 8

slides.note: 2 aur 4 ka test pass? 8 abhi bhi risk mein!

slides.title: Digit-sum test both ways
slides.kicker: One divisibility rule, two if-then sentences
bullets: A shortcut from earlier grades: to check divisibility by 3, add the digits of the number and see if the sum is a multiple of 3.
If-then form 1: if a number is divisible by 3, then the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3.
If-then form 2: if the sum of the digits is a multiple of 3, then the number is divisible by 3.

items: Add the digits of the number
Check if the sum is a multiple of 3

slides.note: Digit jodo, 3 ka test ho gaya!

slides.title: Build Q with sticks
slides.kicker: Two sticks become the diagonals
bullets: We know quadrilateral types — squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombi, kites and trapezia — and we can invent new categories, like Q.
Task: take two thin sticks, put them together as diagonals, and join their endpoints so the quadrilateral obtained is of type Q.
Everything hinges on which if-then property the category Q satisfies.
slides.note: Stick = diagonal. Ab rules ka khel dekho!

slides.title: Rule 1: Q gives equals
slides.kicker: Sticks equal for sure, placement still matters
bullets: Property: if a quadrilateral is of type Q, then it has equal-length diagonals.
So the two sticks must be of equal length — unequal diagonals would rule out type Q at the very start.
But the arrangement still matters: only the forward direction is promised, so equal diagonals alone need not produce type Q.

left.title: Stick lengths
items: Unequal sticks cannot give type Q

right.title: Arrangement
items: How they are put together matters
Equal diagonals alone do not promise Q

slides.note: Rule 1 ek tarafda rasta hai — ulta pakka nahi!

slides.title: Rule 2: equals give Q
slides.kicker: Now equal sticks guarantee success
bullets: Property now: if a quadrilateral has equal diagonals, then it is of type Q.
Keep the sticks of equal length; then every arrangement gives equal diagonals, so every arrangement gives type Q.
So the answers flip from Rule 1: sticks equal, but it does not matter how the two sticks are put together.

left.title: Stick lengths
items: Sticks must be of equal length
Equal diagonals then force type Q

right.title: Arrangement
items: It does not matter how they join

slides.note: Rule 2 mein arrangement free — bas sticks barabar rakho!

slides.title: Four truth patterns
slides.kicker: How P and its converse can behave
bullets: It can happen that a proposition is true while its converse is false — the rain and wet road pair.
Both can be true, like perfect squares and odd factors — or both can be false.
So never trust a converse on credit — test it separately, with a proof or a counterexample.
slides.note: Converse ko apna alag test do — free ka trust nahi!

flashcards.front: What is a proposition?
flashcards.back: A statement that is either true or false, such as: if two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite them are equal.

flashcards.front: How do you form the converse of 'if X then Y'?
flashcards.back: Swap the two parts: the converse is 'if Y then X'. For example, 'if it rains, the road is wet' becomes 'if the road is wet, it has rained'.

flashcards.front: What is a counterexample?
flashcards.back: A situation that illustrates why a proposition is not necessarily true — an example that contradicts the stated proposition.

flashcards.front: What did Euler show about Fermat's prime claim?
flashcards.back: Fermat claimed all numbers of the form 2^(2^n)+1 are prime; Euler disproved it by showing one such number is composite.

flashcards.front: 'X implies Y' is another way of writing what?
flashcards.back: The proposition 'if X then Y'. The book uses both formulations interchangeably.

flashcards.front: What is a partner factor of a factor?
flashcards.back: The factor that multiplies it to give the number: 5 × 7 = 35, so 7 is the partner factor of 5 in 35.

flashcards.front: Name the factor-partner pairs of 12.
flashcards.back: (1, 12), (2, 6) and (3, 4) — each pair multiplies to 12.

flashcards.front: If a number has an odd number of factors, what must be true about it?
flashcards.back: It must be a perfect square: some factor-partner pair repeats as (f, f), so n = f × f.

flashcards.front: Why does a square number have an odd number of factors?
flashcards.back: All factors pair up except one repeating pair (f, f); a number cannot have more than one such repeating pair.

flashcards.front: Are congruent triangles guaranteed to have the same area?
flashcards.back: Yes. But two triangles with the same area need not be congruent, so the converse is false.

flashcards.front: State the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem in if-then form.
flashcards.back: Let a, b, c be the sidelengths of a triangle: if the triangle is right-angled, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

flashcards.front: State the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem.
flashcards.back: Let a, b, c be the sidelengths of a triangle: if a^2 + b^2 = c^2, then the triangle is right-angled.

flashcards.front: Is the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem true?
flashcards.back: Yes. A right triangle with legs a, b has XY = c by the theorem, and SSS congruence then shows ABC is right-angled too.

flashcards.front: What does 'Y when X' mean?
flashcards.back: The same as 'if X then Y'. Example: a number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square.

flashcards.front: What is the incentre of a triangle?
flashcards.back: The point where the angle bisectors meet; the book bisects the angles at B and C, and the bisectors meet at the incentre I.

flashcards.front: State the book's proposition about IE and IF.
flashcards.back: With the bisectors extended to meet the opposite sides at E and F: if AB = AC, then IE = IF.

flashcards.front: Give a counterexample to: n^2 + n + 11 is always prime.
flashcards.back: n = 10 gives 121 = 11 × 11, which is composite, so the claim is false.

flashcards.front: Is 'divisible by 2 and 4' enough to conclude 'divisible by 8'?
flashcards.back: No. For example 12 is divisible by 2 and by 4 but not by 8; the converse of the true proposition fails.

flashcards.front: State the digit rule for 3 as an if-then sentence.
flashcards.back: If a number is divisible by 3, then the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3 — and conversely.

flashcards.front: In the sticks task, what do the two thin sticks represent?
flashcards.back: The diagonals; putting the sticks together as diagonals and joining their endpoints gives a quadrilateral of type Q.

flashcards.front: Q has equal-length diagonals. Must the two sticks be equal?
flashcards.back: Yes. Every type-Q quadrilateral has equal diagonals, so unequal sticks could never build a type-Q quadrilateral.

flashcards.front: If equal diagonals mean type Q, does the sticks arrangement matter?
flashcards.back: No. Any arrangement of equal sticks gives equal diagonals, and that forces type Q.

flashcards.front: Name the truth patterns a proposition P and its converse can show.
flashcards.back: P true while its converse is false, both true, or both false — so test each direction separately.

quiz.q: Which of these is a proposition?
options: What a beautiful rainbow!
If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite them are equal
Please find the value of x
Is 17 a prime number?
quiz.why: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false; the others are an exclamation, a request and a question.

quiz.q: What is the converse of: if it rains, then the road is wet?
options: If it does not rain, then the road is dry
If it rains, then the road is not wet
If the road is wet, then it has rained
If the road is not wet, then it has not rained
quiz.why: Forming the converse swaps the two parts: if Y then X, exactly as in Example 1.

quiz.q: Which number is a counterexample to: every multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6?
quiz.why: 3 is a multiple of 3 but not a multiple of 6, so it contradicts the converse statement Q.

quiz.q: Why is finding a suitable counterexample an important ingredient of mathematics?
options: It proves the converse of the proposition
It shows the proposition holds for most cases
It is useful only when the proposition is about geometry
It shows a proposition is false in a short and convincing way
quiz.why: The book calls a counterexample a short and convincing way to show a proposition is false.

quiz.q: Fermat claimed every number of the form 2^(2^n)+1 is prime. What did Euler's counterexample establish?
options: The claim is false, because one number of that form is composite
257 is not actually of that form
Every number of that form is composite
The converse of the claim must be true
quiz.why: One example that contradicts the claim is enough: Euler showed a number of the form 2^(2^n)+1 is composite.

quiz.q: For the number 35, what is the partner factor of 5?
quiz.why: 5 × 7 = 35, so 7 is the partner factor of 5.

quiz.q: A number has an odd number of factors. What must it be?
options: A prime number
A perfect square
A multiple of 6
An even number
quiz.why: An odd factor count forces a repeating pair (f, f), so the number is n = f × f.

quiz.q: In the pairing argument, why do two repeating pairs like (f, f) and (g, g) matter?
options: They would make the factor count even, but a number cannot have more than one repeating pair
They prove every number has an odd number of factors
They show prime numbers have many partner factors
They only occur in triangles
quiz.why: Two repeating pairs would give an even count, but a number cannot have more than one, so squares end with an odd count.

quiz.q: Which statement about triangles is true?
options: If two triangles have the same area, then they are congruent
If two triangles are congruent, then they have the same area
Equal area always means equal sidelengths
Congruent triangles can have different areas
quiz.why: Congruent triangles have the same area; the same-area-then-congruent direction is the one Example 4 asks us to question.

quiz.q: What is the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem?
options: If a triangle is right-angled, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2
If a^2 + b^2 = c^2, then the triangle is right-angled
If a^2 + b^2 is not c^2, then the triangle is right-angled
If the triangle is not right-angled, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2
quiz.why: Keep the first sentence and flip the second: a^2 + b^2 = c^2 forces a right angle.

quiz.q: 'A number has an odd number of factors when it is a perfect square' means:
options: If a number has an odd number of factors, then it is a perfect square
If a number is a perfect square, then it has an odd number of factors
The two properties are unrelated
Perfect squares never have an odd number of factors
quiz.why: 'Y when X' carries the same meaning as 'if X then Y', as the note in the book explains.

quiz.q: In proving the converse, a right triangle XYZ is built with legs a and b. Why is XY = c?
options: By the SSS criterion
Because XY is the longest side of any triangle
By the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, XY^2 = a^2 + b^2 = c^2
Because congruent triangles have equal hypotenuses
quiz.why: Apply the theorem to the right triangle XYZ: XY^2 = a^2 + b^2 = c^2, so XY = c; SSS comes after.

quiz.q: In triangle ABC, the bisectors of the angles at B and C meet at a special point. Its name?
options: Centroid
Circumcentre
Orthocentre
The incentre I
quiz.why: The book bisects the angles at B and C, and the bisectors meet at the incentre I.

quiz.q: In the book's equation proposition, if x = y, then:
options: a - x = a - y only when a = 0
a + x = a + y, where x, y and a are any three numbers
x + y must equal a
a + x equals y alone
quiz.why: If x = y then a + x = a + y; this proposition and its converse are routinely used while solving equations.

quiz.q: Which value of n is a counterexample to the claim: all numbers of the form n^2 + n + 11 are prime?
quiz.why: 121 = 11 × 11 is composite, so n = 10 contradicts the claim; the other three values give primes.

quiz.q: A number is divisible by 2 and by 4. What follows about divisibility by 8?
options: It must be divisible by 8
It is divisible by 8 only if it is odd
It need not be divisible by 8; for example 12 is not
Divisibility by 8 can never be checked
quiz.why: Divisible by 8 gives divisible by 2 and 4, but the converse fails: 12 is divisible by 2 and 4, not by 8.

quiz.q: To check divisibility by 3, what does the digit shortcut say?
options: Multiply the digits and check the product for 3
Add the digits and check if the sum is a multiple of 3
Subtract the digits repeatedly
Check only the last digit
quiz.why: Add the digits of the number and check whether the sum is a multiple of 3.

quiz.q: Q satisfies: if a quadrilateral is of type Q, then it has equal-length diagonals. What must you ensure while building Q with sticks?
options: Sticks of any lengths, joined in any way
Unequal sticks, joined at the midpoint
Equal sticks, and the arrangement still matters
Equal sticks, joined only at right angles
quiz.why: Type Q forces equal diagonals, so sticks must be equal; but equal diagonals alone does not promise type Q.

quiz.q: Now Q satisfies: if a quadrilateral has equal diagonals, then it is of type Q. How should you place two equal sticks?
options: Only one special arrangement works
Any arrangement works, since equal diagonals then force type Q
They must be unequal first, then made equal
The arrangement matters as much as the length
quiz.why: Equal diagonals guarantee type Q, so it does not matter how the two sticks are put together.

quiz.q: Which pattern can a proposition P and its converse show?
options: Only both true
Only both false
P true with converse false, both true, or both false
Always exactly one of them is true
quiz.why: The chapter closes: true with a false converse, both true, or both false can all happen.

examples.title: Converse check for multiples
examples.problem: Consider the proposition P: if a number is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3. Justify P, then determine whether its converse Q is true, giving a counterexample if it is not.
steps: Write P with symbols: if n is a multiple of 6, then n = 6 × k for some whole number k.
Rewrite n = 3 × (2 × k), which shows n is a multiple of 3, so proposition P is true.
The converse Q says: if a number is a multiple of 3, then it is a multiple of 6. Test the smallest multiple of 3.
Take 3: it equals 3 × 1, but 3 is not a multiple of 6, so 3 is a counterexample and Q is false.
examples.answer: P is true; its converse Q is false, with 3 as a counterexample.

examples.title: Odd factors meet perfect squares
examples.problem: Use factor-partner pairs to show that 25 has an odd number of factors while 12 does not, and connect this to the perfect square property.
steps: Pair the factors of 12: (1, 12), (2, 6) and (3, 4). Every factor has a distinct partner, so 12 has 6 factors, an even number.
Pair the factors of 25: (1, 25) and (5, 5). Here 5 is its own partner, so the pair (5, 5) repeats.
The factors of 25 are 1, 5 and 25 — that is 3 factors, an odd number, and 25 = 5 × 5 is a perfect square.
Generalise: an odd factor count means one repeating pair (f, f), so n = f × f; and a square has exactly one such pair, so its factor count is odd.
examples.answer: 12 has an even number of factors and is not a square; 25 has an odd number of factors and is a perfect square — each fact implies the other.

examples.title: Proving the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras converse
examples.problem: Let a, b, c be the sidelengths of a triangle ABC with a^2 + b^2 = c^2. Show that triangle ABC is right-angled.
steps: Construct a right-angled triangle XYZ whose legs a and b meet at the right angle.
Apply the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem to XYZ: the hypotenuse satisfies XY^2 = a^2 + b^2.
Since a^2 + b^2 = c^2, we get XY^2 = c^2, so XY = c.
Now triangle ABC and triangle XYZ both have sidelengths a, b, c, so they are congruent by the SSS criterion.
The congruence matches the right angle of XYZ with the corresponding angle of ABC, so ABC had to be a right triangle after all.
examples.answer: The converse is true: if a^2 + b^2 = c^2, then the triangle is right-angled.

examples.title: Counterexample hunt for prime claims
examples.problem: Find counterexamples to two claims from the exercise: (i) all numbers of the form n^2 + n + 11 are prime; (ii) if n is a prime number, then 2^n - 1 is a prime number.
steps: For claim (i), compute n^2 + n + 11 for small n: n = 1 gives 13, n = 3 gives 23, n = 5 gives 41 — all prime so far.
At n = 10: 10^2 + 10 + 11 = 121 = 11 × 11, which is composite. So n = 10 is a counterexample and claim (i) is false.
For claim (ii), test prime n: n = 2 gives 3, n = 3 gives 7, n = 5 gives 31 — all prime so far.
At n = 11: 2^11 - 1 = 2048 - 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89, which is composite. So n = 11 is a counterexample and claim (ii) is false.
examples.answer: Claim (i) falls at n = 10, where 121 is composite; claim (ii) falls at n = 11, where 2047 is composite.

steps.label: Meet a proposition
steps.detail: A statement that is either true or false, written as if X then Y.

steps.label: Frame the converse
steps.detail: Swap the parts to get if Y then X, like the two triangle statements.

steps.label: Test proposition P
steps.detail: Justify true statements with a proof, as with multiples of 6 and 3.

steps.label: Hunt counterexamples
steps.detail: One contradicting example, like the wet road from a tanker, fells a false claim.

steps.label: Compare P and Q
steps.detail: Both true, one true, or both false — each pattern can occur.

steps.label: Explore number patterns
steps.detail: Factor-partner pairs link perfect squares with odd numbers of factors.

steps.label: Explore geometry links
steps.detail: The converse of Baudhāyana–Pythagoras is proved using SSS congruence.

steps.label: Apply with care
steps.detail: Use if-then reasoning in equations, divisibility checks and stick constructions.
